entries.title: What does the U.S. National Archives keep?
entries.answer: The U.S. National Archives takes care of records made by the national government that have lasting value. Some are famous, such as the signed Declaration of Independence. Other records help people learn about their families or communities. They can look at old census records, maps, and photographs. An archive keeps evidence of what happened. Archivists organize these records so people can find them, and they protect fragile pieces from damage so future readers can study them too.
facts: Government records can be pictures, recordings, maps, or digital files as well as pages of text.
The National Archives keeps the original signed U.S. Constitution.

entries.title: What goes on behind the scenes in a museum?
entries.answer: A museum collects and cares for objects that can teach people something. A museum might hold paintings, historic clothing, fossils, or dried plants. Only part of a big collection fits in the rooms visitors can walk through. Staff also measure, photograph, label, and store objects so they can be found and studied later. A conservator helps protect fragile things. If a piece of cloth can fade in bright light, for example, a museum may show it only under dim light for part of the year.
facts: The objects a museum has gathered and cares for form its collection.
Researchers can study some objects that are kept in storage.

entries.title: What is the Library of Congress?
entries.answer: The Library of Congress is a research library in Washington, D.C. It helps people in Congress find information they need and also makes materials available to the public. Books are only part of what it keeps. Its collections include maps, photographs, sound recordings, and music. A catalog helps people look up what the library has and where to find it. The library also runs a service that makes books available in forms such as braille and audio for eligible readers.
facts: The Library of Congress began in 1800.
Some library materials can be viewed online away from Washington, D.C.
